Last week we compared teams by their average scoring margin.

This week we'll try some new ways of visualizing that data.

## Load packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse) # You should already have installed this package in previous weeks
source("helper-functions.R") # This is a place where you will paste useful functions to reuse
```

## Import data

```{r}
games <- read_csv("data/games_2025.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## Recreate the team summary

A little review from last week!

Below is the code. You should write the verbal description of the code here:

1. START with games
2. THEN

```{r}
games |>
  select(season, home_team, away_team, home_score, away_score) |>
  filter(season == 2025, !is.na(home_score), !is.na(away_score)) -> completed_games
```

1. START with completed_games
2. THEN

```{r}
completed_games |>
  select(season, team = home_team, opponent = away_team,
         points_scored = home_score, points_allowed = away_score) |>
  mutate(venue = "Home") -> home_team_games
```


1. START with completed_games
2. THEN

```{r}
completed_games |>
  select(season, team = away_team, opponent = home_team,
         points_scored = away_score, points_allowed = home_score) |>
  mutate(venue = "Away") -> away_team_games
```

1. START with home_team_games
2. THEN

```{r}
home_team_games |>
  bind_rows(away_team_games) |>
  mutate(scoring_margin = points_scored - points_allowed) -> team_games
```

1. START with team_games
2. THEN

```{r}
team_games |>
  group_by(team) |>
  summarise(games_played = n(),
            average_scoring_margin = mean(scoring_margin),
            .groups = "drop") -> team_summary
```

## Start with a basic plot

1. START with team_summary
2. THEN pass the data to GGPLOT WITH team on the x-axis and average_scoring margin on y-axis
3. ADD GEOM_POINT to show all the dots WITH color = RED and size = 1
4. ADD LABS to show labels WITH title = "NFL", x = "Team" and y = "Value"
5. ADD THEME_GRAY

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

team_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = team, y = average_scoring_margin)) +
  geom_point(color = "red", size = 1) +
  labs(title = "NFL", x = "Team", y = "Value") +
  theme_gray()
```

Before changing the figure:

- How could we make it easier to find the team with the highest scoring margin?
- What other changes could make this graph clearer?

## Now let's build the plot one layer at a time

This is how you will build all your plots in R: One layer at a time.

Basically, add a layer, see how it looks, then make adjustments or add another layer

### 1. Create the axes but don't show any data

1. START with team_summary.
2. THEN pass it to ggplot().
3. Use aes() to put average scoring margin on the x-axis and team on the y-axis.

```{r}
team_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = average_scoring_margin, y = team))
```

### 2. Add a geometry layer

This is usually some sort of way of showing the data. Bar chart, dots, violin plots, box plots, etc

Complete this:

1. START with team_summary
2. THEN

```{r}
team_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = average_scoring_margin, y = team)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, color = "#176B87")
```

Run this chunk a few times.

Try changing `size` and `shape`.

If you're not sure how to change the shape, try searching in the help tab or try searching stackoverflow.

Obviously, I've already chosen the ideal color so no need to experiment there.

### 3. Order the teams

Complete this:

1. START with team_summary
2. THEN

```{r}
team_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = average_scoring_margin,
             y = reorder(team, average_scoring_margin))) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, color = "#176B87")
```

`reorder()` changes the order of the team labels using their average margins.
The highest value appears at the top.

### 4. Add a vertical line and a theme

Complete this:

1. START with team_summary
2. THEN


```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8

team_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = average_scoring_margin,
             y = reorder(team, average_scoring_margin))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey65", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, color = "#176B87") +
  labs(title = "Average scoring margin by NFL team",
       subtitle = "2025 regular season; each team played 17 games",
       x = "Average scoring margin (points per game)",
       y = NULL,
       caption = "Data: nflverse/nfldata via nflreadr; 2025 regular season") +
  theme_nfl_lab()
```

Keep experimenting with different themes until you find one you like!

## Map a color to a specific team

1. START with team_summary.
2. MUTATE a new variable indicating whether each row is your selected team.
3. STORE the result in highlighted_teams.

Replace "JAX" with another team abbreviation from the data if you prefer.

```{r}
selected_team <- "JAX"

team_summary |>
  mutate(highlight = if_else(team == selected_team,
                            "Selected team", "Other teams")) -> highlighted_teams

highlighted_teams
```
Click through the above data until you can confirm that JAX (or your team) is the 'selected team'

1. START with highlighted_teams
2. THEN

```{r}
highlighted_teams |>
  ggplot(aes(x = average_scoring_margin,
             y = reorder(team, average_scoring_margin))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey65", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(color = highlight, shape = highlight), size = 2.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Other teams" = "grey60",
                                "Selected team" = "#176B87")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Other teams" = 16, "Selected team" = 17)) +
  labs(title = paste("Where does", selected_team, "fall in the comparison?"),
       subtitle = "2025 regular season",
       x = "Average scoring margin (points per game)", y = NULL,
       color = NULL, shape = NULL,
       caption = "Data: nflverse/nfldata via nflreadr; 2025 regular season") +
  theme_nfl_lab() -> highlight_plot
```

### Quick coloring tip

When you put 'color' inside 'aes', you decide which variable determines the colors.

But when you put color on its own (or outside aes) then every 'point' gets the same color.

Notice that 'scale_color_manual' is where we set the actual colors that appear in the graph.

We have a variable called 'highlight' with two values: 'Other teams' and 'Selected team'

We use scale_color_manual to tell ggplot which color each value of 'highlight' should get

So, we could add more values to 'highlight' and add more color decisions to scale_color_manual


### Also, notice we can save a ggplot into a variable and then use it in future code

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8
highlight_plot
```

Note that changing the shape means that the graph doesn't depend on color alone which means it is more color-blind friendly

## Optional: compare home and away performance

Now change the question: does each team's average margin look different at home and away?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

team_games |>
  group_by(team, venue) |>
  summarise(average_scoring_margin = mean(scoring_margin),
            games_played = n(), .groups = "drop") -> venue_summary

# Keep the same team order in both panels, based on the full-season summary.
team_summary |>
  arrange(average_scoring_margin, team) |>
  pull(team) -> team_order

venue_summary |>
  mutate(team = factor(team, levels = team_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = average_scoring_margin, y = team)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey65", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(color = "#176B87", size = 2.4) +
  facet_wrap(~venue) +
  labs(title = "Compare scoring margins at home and away",
       subtitle = "2025 regular season; panels use the same axes and team order",
       x = "Average scoring margin (points per game)", y = NULL,
       caption = "Data: nflverse/nfldata via nflreadr; 2025 regular season") +
  theme_nfl_lab()
```

Check `venue_summary` for games played. Teams played different numbers of home and away games. Opponents also differed, so these panels alone do not show that venue caused a difference.

## Save your figure to your computer

After creating `my_plot`, enable this chunk by changing `eval: false` to `eval: true`.
Save your plot into a variable called 'my_plot' and then run.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggsave("week-03-my-plot.png", plot = my_plot,
       width = 9, height = 8, units = "in", dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```
